params.text:
Balancing safety with rights and choices

People have the right to make their own decisions about their lives — including decisions that carry some risk. This is sometimes called the dignity of risk: being allowed to take everyday risks is part of living a full and dignified life. A person who is never allowed to try, to fail, or to make an unwise choice is being denied their independence. It can feel safest to stop the people you support from doing anything risky, yet a life with no risk is often a life with no choice, independence or enjoyment.

This can sit in tension with your duty of care. Your instinct may be to protect someone from every possible harm, but over-protecting a person can strip away their confidence, dignity and self-worth. Your duty of care sits alongside each person's right to make their own decisions, and the skill lies in finding a balance.

Positive risk-taking

Positive risk-taking is how we manage that balance. It means working with a person to weigh up the benefits and the hazards of an activity, then supporting them to do what they want to do as safely as possible — sensibly assessing and reducing the risks, rather than simply saying "no".

Unwise decisions and mental capacity

The Mental Capacity Act 2005 is clear that a person who has capacity is allowed to make what others might see as an unwise decision. Choosing to eat foods a dietitian advised against, or to walk to the shops alone, is their right.

  • Start by assuming capacity: do not treat a choice as unsafe just because you disagree with it.
  • Share clear, honest information: make sure the person understands the likely benefits and dangers.
  • Listen and respect their wishes: pay attention to what matters to them.
  • Plan together: work with the person, their family and the wider team to agree a plan and a risk assessment, taking small steps that reduce danger without removing the choice.
  • Record the decision: note the discussion, the risks discussed and the agreed support, so the reasoning is clear to others.

Remember that a person who has mental capacity has the right to make a decision that others might consider unwise. Your role is to support the choice safely, not to overrule it.

params.alt: A care worker sitting with an older person they support, beside the heading “Balancing safety with rights and choices”. Key points: Start by assuming capacity; Share clear, honest information; Listen and respect their wishes.

params.question: A person with mental capacity may make a decision you consider unwise, and your role is to support them to do it as safely as possible rather than to overrule them.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. Under the Mental Capacity Act, a person with capacity has the right to make unwise decisions, and positive risk-taking supports them to do so safely.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The Mental Capacity Act protects a capable person’s right to make unwise decisions; your job is to reduce risk, not remove the choice.
